nodes.label: Goldman et al. (1971) described adolescent cystinosis and compared it with the infantile and adult forms of cystinosis.
Spear et al. (1971) described polykaryocytosis (multinucleated cells) of the visceral glomerular epithelium in cystinosis, and described an unusual clinical variant of cystinosis.
Abnormal glomerular visceral epithelial cell morphology
Langman et al. (1985) reported renal failure in a sibship with late-onset cystinosis.

Thoene et al. (1999) described 6 patients with the intermediate form of cystinosis and identified CTNS mutations, 2 of which had not been reported before. They found that the disease resulted either from compound heterozygosity for one mild mutation and one mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or from homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.

Thoene et al. (1999) concluded that intermediate cystinosis results from having at least one mild CTNS mutation: either one mild mutation together with a mutation that causes nephropathic cystinosis, or two copies (homozygosity) of a predicted mild mutation.

Thoene et al. (1999) showed that transfecting cystinotic fibroblasts with normal CTNS cDNA, or with a cDNA carrying a mutation that causes intermediate cystinosis, partially corrected the cells' phenotype.
Attard et al. (1999) described late-onset cystinosis as a rarer form of the disorder, characterized by onset of symptoms between 12 and 15 years of age.

Attard et al. (1999) screened the CTNS gene in patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, patients with late-onset cystinosis, and patients whose phenotype did not fit the classical definitions. They found 23 different CTNS mutations, 14 of them novel. In 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis, the mutations affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin, which the authors concluded accounted for the milder phenotype.

Attard et al. (1999) found that 3 patients had cystinosis onset before 7 years of age but a milder course than the infantile nephropathic form. These patients carried missense mutations in CTNS. The authors suggested that these mutations allow production of functional protein and may mark regions of cystinosin that are not functionally important.

Attard et al. (1999) reported that of 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, 12 had 2 severely truncating CTNS mutations, consistent with loss of functional protein. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions, predicted to disrupt transmembrane domains and abolish protein function.
Macías-Vidal et al. (2009) analyzed the CTNS gene in 32 patients with cystinosis from Spain.
